newsitem.title: TURKEY: Gazprom seeks $3 bln credit for Turkey pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom seeks $3 bln credit for Turkey pipeline.

text.p: Russian gas monopoly Gazprom said on Wednesday that credit worth $3 billion would be sought for a planned underwater gas pipeline linking Russia and Turkey via the Black Sea.

"The project will cost $3 billion which will be met through credits... We are looking mainly to European banks," Gazprom board member Vladimir Rezunenko told Reuters after attending a briefing on the project in the Turkish capital.

He said Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas company, and Turkey's state pipeline company Botas were currently carrying out feasibility studies for the pipeline which are expected to be completed by June.
Rezunenko said the venture planned to begin gas deliveries by the year 2000 under the project, which is being overseen by a joint venture with the Dutch firm Heerema.
Gas deliveries via the pipeline are targeted to begin with three billion cubic metres (bcm) in the year 2000, rising to 16 bcm by 2010.
Turkey receives six bcm of gas from Russia via an existing pipeline through Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria. Rezunenko said it was planned to raise deliveries to Turkey through this pipeline to 14 bcm.
"We have reached agreement in talks with Botas to raise annual gas delivery to 30 billion cubic metres," Rezunenko said.
The Black Sea pipeline in total will be 1,200 km (750 mile) long from Izobilnoye, 100 km (63 miles) east of Krasnodar in southern Russia, to the Turkish capital Ankara.
A 385 km (240 mile) stretch of the pipeline will pass under the Black Sea from the Russian outlet of Dzhugba to Turkey's Samsun port and another 440 km (279 mile) line will link Samsun and Ankara.
The pipeline will be the deepest in the world and may have to go as deep as 2,100 metres under the sea in some places, Botas officials say.
The deepest pipeline project in the world at present is at a depth of 1,640 metres being carried out for Shell in the Gulf of Mexico.
Rezunenko said Gazprom was also proposing the delivery of three bcm of gas via an overland pipeline through Georgia and Armenia to eastern Turkey.
Renovation and extension of existing pipelines under this project would cost $146 million. Botas has not reached a decision on this project.
Botas general manager Mustafa Murathan told the briefing in Ankara that Turkey's energy demand was rising 10-12 percent annually and could not be met by existing resources.
He said the rising demand would requiire increasing gas supplies to 35 bcm by the year 2001 and to 55-58 bcm by 2010.
Turkey also has gas delivery accords with Iran, Algeria, Nigeria, Qatar, Turkmenistan and Yemen.
A 23-year, $23 billion accord with Iran under which Turkey plans to import three bcm form 1998, rising to 10 bcm from 2005, has drawn criticism from its NATO ally, the United States.
